articles.title: BENOIT ON CCD'S
articles.summary: At a recent meeting, amateur CCD imager Benoit Schillings discussed his pioneering work on adaptive optics for amateur astronomy. Driven by a challenge to achieve sub-arcsecond resolution, Schillings developed a DIY adaptive optical guiding system that significantly improved image tightness for modest aperture instruments. His refined 'Mark II' system was later adopted and sold by SBIG, demonstrating a significant advancement in amateur imaging technology.

articles.title: JULY
articles.summary: The document provides a detailed schedule of astronomical events and meetings for the month of July. It lists several star parties at Houge Park and Fremont Peak, along with a general meeting at Houge Park. Each star party entry includes useful observing information such as sunset times and moon phase/set/rise times.

articles.title: AUGUST
articles.summary: The August schedule for the San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA) features a "Planetary Observing" class, a general meeting with a presentation on "The Wonders of Jupiter" by Jose Olivarez, and multiple star parties at Houge Park, Fremont Peak, and Coe. The document also provides contact information and an important note regarding SJAA insurance coverage for members.

articles.title: THE CELESTIAL TOURIST SPEAKS
articles.summary: Jay Freeman, 'The Celestial Tourist,' recounts his profound experience observing the quasar 3C273 in the early 1980s, reflecting on its immense cosmological distance and the ancient origin of its light. He also reviews the movie 'Deep Impact,' finding it to be a 'pretty good' dramatization of humanity's response to a potential comet impact, despite not being 'excellent science fiction'.

articles.title: Perseis, from p. 1
articles.summary: An adaptive optic guider significantly improves image quality for amateur astronomers by correcting mount imperfections, especially for longer exposures, reducing image spread by half. While less effective for short-exposure lunar and planetary CCD imaging, a new program is being developed to enhance results in those areas. The article praises Benoit's insightful and engaging presentation on the topic, highlighting his expertise in CCD work.

articles.title: Tourist, from p. 1
articles.summary: This article reviews a science fiction production, likely a film, evaluating its scientific details and plot elements. The reviewer notes that while some scientific lapses were present for dramatization, the overall accuracy was decent for the genre, avoiding major scientific blunders often seen in such cinema.

articles.title: PERIODICAL PUBLICATION STATEMENT
articles.summary: The 'SJAA Ephemeris,' the official newsletter of the San Jose Astronomical Association, is published monthly, totaling 12 issues per year, from January through December. The statement also provides the full postal address for the San Jose Astronomical Association.

articles.title: Akkana Peck
articles.summary: The article provides an astronomical guide for July, highlighting the return of Jupiter and Saturn to the night sky, along with their key observational events like Jupiter's retrograde motion and a double moon shadow transit. It also details the visibility of Mercury, Venus, Mars, and the dim outer planets (Uranus, Neptune, Pluto), and mentions the peak of the Delta-Aquarid meteor shower.

articles.title: David North
articles.summary: This article is a personal report from a representative attending the RTMC astronomy convention, detailing the event's atmosphere, challenges, and highlights. The author describes the dusty mountain location, parking difficulties, but praises the abundance of unique amateur-built telescopes and the inspiring community of astronomy enthusiasts. Specific innovative telescope designs, such as an f/40 refractor, a split-ring mount, and various Dobsonian and portable designs, are noted as key attractions of the event.

articles.title: RTMC, from p. 2
articles.summary: This article provides a brief recap of an event, highlighting various telescope manufacturers and vendors showcasing their innovations. The author mentions specific companies like Starsplitter, Celestron, Pocono, and Mountain Instruments, noting interesting products and designs. The event offered a valuable opportunity to see new inventory and connect with people in the astronomy community.

articles.title: David North
articles.summary: This article details celestial observation opportunities for July, primarily focusing on lunar events. It highlights a rare chance to view Mare Orientale during a full Moon on July 8th/9th due to maximum western limb libration, and mentions the smallest Moon of the year around July 4th. The author also notes close approaches by Jupiter and Saturn, two first-quarter Moons, and good conditions for observing eastern lunar features like Mare Crisium.

articles.title: David North
articles.summary: This article discusses the personal benefits of using an observer's eye patch for enhanced stargazing comfort. It also provides an update on the Fremont Peak Observatory's 30" Challenger Telescope, which is back in operation after repairs and is awaiting further upgrades like custom focusers and light baffles. Additionally, it notes the lack of a quorum at a recent board meeting and the rescheduling of an astrophotography class to September.

articles.title: Don Machholz
articles.summary: This article details recent comet discoveries, including Comet 1998 K1 (Mueller) and three LINEAR comets initially found as asteroidal objects with comae or tails. It also analyzes the declination ranges where amateur astronomers typically discover comets, providing a statistical breakdown for both hemispheres. Additionally, the document includes ephemerides for several notable comets like C/1997 J2 (Meunier-Dupouy), C/1995 O1 (Hale-Bopp), and C/1998 J1 (SOHO) for July and early August.

articles.title: Orbital Elements
articles.summary: This document presents a table detailing the orbital elements for three celestial objects: Comet Hale-Bopp, Comet Meunier-Dupouy, and SOHO. Key parameters listed include perihelion date and distance, argument of perihelion, ascending node, inclination, eccentricity, orbital period, and absolute magnitude, offering a comparative overview of their trajectories.

articles.title: SUBMIT
articles.summary: The SJAA *Ephemeris* newsletter encourages members to submit articles for publication. Submissions, which should include the author's name and phone number, must be sent via email to Dave North at Timocharis@aol.com by the tenth of each month to be included in the following month's issue.

articles.title: Lunar Phase Time
articles.summary: This document provides a table detailing the timing of major lunar phases for a given month, including First Quarter (FQ), Full Moon (FM), Last Quarter (LQ), and New Moon (NM). For each phase, it lists the time, date, moonrise time, transit time, and moonset time, with all times specified in Pacific Daylight Time (PDT).

articles.title: Mercury

It lists daily rise, transit, and set times, along with its Right Ascension and Declination for the 7th, 17th, and 27th of the month, serving as a guide for observers.

articles.title: Venus

articles.title: Mars

It lists Mars's distance from Earth (2.5 AU), apparent magnitude (+1.5), and its rise, transit, and set times, along with its right ascension (R.A.) and declination (Dec.) for each date.

articles.title: Jupiter
articles.summary: This document provides an ephemeris for Jupiter, listing its magnitude, distance, and daily rise, transit, and set times for various dates. It also includes the planet's Right Ascension and Declination, making it a useful resource for astronomical observers.

articles.title: Saturn
articles.summary: This document provides an astronomical ephemeris for Saturn, detailing its observable characteristics and positional data over a period of three dates. It includes its magnitude, distance in A.U., daily rise, transit, and set times, along with its Right Ascension and Declination.

articles.title: SOL/Star Type G2V Intelligent Life in System?
articles.summary: The article presents a speculative question regarding the existence of intelligent life within a SOL/Star Type G2V system. Following this intriguing title, it provides a table of astronomical data, including hours of darkness, rise/transit/set times, right ascension, and declination across several dates, which appears to be observational or ephemeris data.

articles.title: Astronomical Twilight
articles.summary: This document provides a tabular listing of astronomical twilight start and end times for specific Julian Dates (JD). It details how these times vary across different dates, offering a schedule for when astronomical twilight begins and concludes.

It lists the "Transit Right Ascension at Local Midnight" for specific numerical values (07, 17, 27) at 00:00, showing corresponding sidereal times of 17:52, 18:31, and 19:11. This data likely serves as a reference or an example for understanding sidereal time calculations.

articles.title: Darkest Saturday Night 25-Jul-98
articles.summary: This document details the astronomical timings for "Darkest Saturday Night" on July 25, 1998. It lists crucial times such as sunset, twilight end, moon set, dawn begin, and the total hours of darkness available for optimal stargazing.

articles.title: ACTIVITIES THROUGH OTHER CLUBS
articles.summary: This article outlines astronomy observing activities and events hosted by various clubs. TAC offers indefinite Wednesday observing at Montebello (requiring a permit holder and website check), as well as mobile First Quarter Friday star parties and Third Quarter Friday star parties at Van Meter school. PAS provides public viewing at Foothill Observatory every clear Friday evening and solar viewing every clear Saturday morning, encouraging SJAA members to attend.

articles.title: July
articles.summary: The article outlines the Palo Alto Astronomical Society's (PAS) activities for July and August, including general meetings and board meetings held at Foothill College. It also details a series of star parties scheduled at Foothill Park, providing dates, times, and instructions for public participation and telescope owners. These events are primarily held on Saturday evenings, with specific parking and entry information provided.

articles.title: STANFORD SEMINARS
articles.summary: Stanford University is hosting a summer seminar series titled 'New Science and Technology in the Aerospace Age' on Thursdays at Terman Auditorium. The series features speakers from NASA Ames Research Center and SETI, covering topics such as space missions, infrared astronomy, air traffic management, and the search for life beyond Earth. All SJAA members are invited to attend these free presentations.
